articles.title: Munich Biennale 2025 Program Announced: 24 World Premieres
articles.author: Festival Team
articles.excerpt: We're thrilled to unveil the complete program for Munich Biennale 2025, featuring 24 groundbreaking world premieres across opera, music theatre, performance, and installation.
articles.body:
After months of anticipation, we're thrilled to unveil the complete program for Munich Biennale 2025. Running from May 15 to June 30, this year's festival features 24 productions spanning opera, music theatre, performance art, and installation—16 of which are world premieres.

## A Festival of Innovation

This year's program reflects our commitment to pushing the boundaries of contemporary music theatre. From Sarah Chen's technologically immersive opera 'The Vanishing Point' to Yuki Tanaka's site-specific performance installation 'Liquid Architectures,' each work represents a unique vision of what music theatre can be in the 21st century.

Artistic Director Mara Fischer notes: 'We've assembled a program that doesn't shy away from the urgent questions of our time—climate change, artificial intelligence, social transformation, cultural memory. But these works approach these themes through the lens of artistic innovation, creating experiences that are as emotionally powerful as they are intellectually stimulating.'

## International Collaborations

The 2025 program brings together artists from 23 countries across five continents. Highlighting the festival's commitment to international exchange, several productions emerged from multi-year collaborative processes involving artists, scientists, and researchers from diverse fields.

Notable collaborations include the partnership with the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research on 'The Vanishing Point,' the ZKM Center for Art and Media's technical support for 'Liquid Architectures,' and the involvement of the Ars Electronica Futurelab in multiple projects.

## Access and Accessibility

We're proud to announce enhanced accessibility features across all venues, including audio description, sign language interpretation, and sensory-friendly performances. Student rush tickets will be available for €10 one hour before each performance, and our expanded community engagement program offers free workshops and open rehearsals throughout the festival period.

## Tickets on Sale Now

Tickets are available now through our website and at the festival box office. Early booking is recommended, as several productions have already reached 70% capacity. Festival passes offering access to multiple performances are available at a reduced rate.

Join us for what promises to be our most ambitious and exciting festival yet.

articles.title: In Conversation: Sarah Chen on 'The Vanishing Point'
articles.author: Julia Schneider
articles.excerpt: Composer Sarah Chen discusses her ambitious new opera exploring technology and consciousness, premiering at this year's festival.
articles.body:
Ahead of the world premiere of 'The Vanishing Point' at Munich Biennale 2025, composer Sarah Chen spoke with us about the three-year journey of creating this ambitious work that sits at the intersection of opera, technology, and neuroscience.

**Julia Schneider: Your opera explores the idea of uploading human consciousness to a digital substrate. What drew you to this subject?**

Sarah Chen: I've been fascinated by questions of consciousness and identity for years, but what really catalyzed this project was reading about the work being done in brain-computer interfaces and neural mapping. There's this moment we're approaching where these technologies might actually become possible, and I wanted to explore what that means not just technologically, but emotionally, philosophically, even spiritually.

What interested me wasn't the science fiction spectacle of it, but the deeply human questions underneath. If you could preserve your consciousness, would you still be you? What would you lose in translation? These are fundamentally operatic questions—questions of identity, transformation, mortality.

**JS: How did you approach integrating electronic and acoustic elements in the score?**

SC: The score needed to embody the journey from purely human to human-digital hybrid. We start with a traditional chamber orchestra—very organic, very physical. As the protagonist Ada's consciousness begins to interface with the digital system, electronic processing gradually infiltrates the orchestral sound.

But it's not a simple binary. The electronic elements aren't cold or alienating—they're extensions of the human voice, the human breath. I worked closely with IRCAM in Paris on spectral analysis techniques that let us transform acoustic sounds in ways that feel like natural evolution rather than artificial imposition.

By the opera's climax, you can't tell where the orchestra ends and the electronics begin. That ambiguity is the point.

**JS: You collaborated with science fiction author Liu Cixin on the libretto. How did that partnership work?**

SC: Liu brought a rigor to the scientific and philosophical concepts that I couldn't have achieved alone. He's thought deeply about these questions in his novels, but he also understood that opera operates differently than prose fiction. We needed to find emotional truth through poetry and music, not exposition.

The libretto went through many iterations. Liu would propose these beautiful, complex ideas, and then we'd work together to distill them into something that could be sung, that could carry emotional weight. Sometimes a single line would represent weeks of discussion.

**JS: The production involves some cutting-edge staging technology. How involved were you in those aspects?**

SC: Very involved. Director Marcus Weber and I were aligned from the beginning that the visual and sonic elements needed to be completely integrated. We worked with media artist Ryoji Ikeda on the projection system, which uses real-time motion capture to create generative visuals that respond to the performers' movements and the music.

There were technical challenges—making sure the performers could hear the orchestra properly while wearing motion capture suits, syncing the electronics with the visual system. But these challenges forced us to think differently about the relationship between singer, space, and sound.

**JS: What do you hope audiences take away from 'The Vanishing Point'?**

SC: I hope they're moved. Beyond all the technology and concepts, this is a story about a person facing mortality, making an impossible choice, and discovering what it means to be human by risking losing their humanity.

If the opera succeeds, people will leave asking questions—about consciousness, about identity, about what we're willing to sacrifice for survival or transcendence. But they'll be asking these questions emotionally, not just intellectually. That's the power of opera.

---

*'The Vanishing Point' premieres May 15 at Muffathalle, with additional performances May 16-18. Tickets are available now.*
